<properties>
{"title":"40. Parity, time reversal, and charge conjugation"}
</properties>
<content>
Recall that, under a Lorentz transformation $`\Lambda`$ implemented by the unitary operator $`U ( \Lambda )`$ , a Dirac (or Majorana) field transforms as
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#7915531691314fee92ce85f594e38819">
	$$
	U ( \Lambda ) ^ { - 1 } \Psi ( x ) U ( \Lambda ) = D ( \Lambda ) \Psi ( \Lambda ^ { - 1 } x ) . \tag{40.1}
	$$
</synced_block>
For an infinitesimal transformation $`\Lambda ^ { \mu } { } _ { \nu } = \delta ^ { \mu } { } _ { \nu } + \delta \omega ^ { \mu } { } _ { \nu }`$ , the matrix $`D ( \Lambda )`$ is given by
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#3e78d217b33444e9a9fb3b8cb98b20bc">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r } { D ( 1 + \delta \omega ) = I + \frac { i } { 2 } \delta \omega _ { \mu \nu } S ^ { \mu \nu } , } \end{array} \tag{40.2}
	$$
</synced_block>
where the Lorentz generator matrices are
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#fffcfe83f9a846c597ded3fec6910b8d">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r } { S ^ { \mu \nu } = \frac { i } { 4 } [ \gamma ^ { \mu } , \gamma ^ { \nu } ] . } \end{array} \tag{40.3}
	$$
</synced_block>
In this section, we will consider the two Lorentz transformations that cannot be reached via a sequence of infinitesimal transformations away from the identity: parity and time reversal. We begin with parity.
Define the parity transformation
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#e0ff20eae91d484ba392ca3bc3d6361a">
	$$
	\mathcal { P } ^ { \mu } { } _ { \nu } = ( \mathcal { P } ^ { - 1 } ) ^ { \mu } { } _ { \nu } = \left( \begin{array} { c c c c } { { + 1 } } & { { } } & { { } } & { { } } \\{ { } } & { { - 1 } } & { { } } & { { } } \\{ { } } & { { } } & { { - 1 } } & { { } } \\{ { } } & { { } } & { { } } & { { - 1 } } \end{array} \right) \tag{40.4}
	$$
</synced_block>
and the corresponding unitary operator
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#7c365feafd0346fe937db98f4621fe47">
	$$
	P \equiv U ( \mathscr { P } ) . \tag{40.5}
	$$
</synced_block>
Now we have
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#2aeca01c439f4227b5fe18a86847a9dc">
	$$
	P ^ { - 1 } \Psi ( x ) P = D ( \mathcal P ) \Psi ( \mathcal P x ) . \tag{40.6}
	$$
</synced_block>
The question we wish to answer is, what is the matrix $`D ( \mathcal { P } )`$ ?
First of all, if we make a second parity transformation, we get
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#5f12e54074254269a24275aa473a1dd5">
	$$
	P ^ { - 2 } \Psi ( x ) P ^ { 2 } = D ( \mathcal P ) ^ { 2 } \Psi ( x ) , \tag{40.7}
	$$
</synced_block>
and it is tempting to conclude that we should have $`D ( \mathcal { P } ) ^ { 2 } = 1`$ , so that we return to the original field. This is correct for scalar fields, since they are themselves observable. With fermions, however, it takes an even number of fields to construct an observable. Therefore we need only require the weaker condition $`D ( \mathcal { P } ) ^ { 2 } = \pm 1`$ .
We will also require the particle creation and annihilation operators to transform in a simple way. Because
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#793f0a36f583437b8610e0e691408a30">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r } { P ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { P } P = - \mathbf { P } \ , } \\{ P ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { J } P = + \mathbf { J } \ , } \end{array} \tag{40.8-40.9}
	$$
</synced_block>
where $`\mathbf { P }`$ is the total three-momentum operator and $`\mathbf { J }`$ is the total angular momentum operator, a parity transformation should reverse the threemomentum while leaving the spin direction unchanged. We therefore require
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#1487c2cd47574580a2aea08438348f2b">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r l r } & { } & { P ^ { - 1 } b _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) P = \eta b _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf - p } ) , } \\& { } & \\& { } & { P ^ { - 1 } d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) P = \eta d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf - p } ) , } \end{array} \tag{40.10}
	$$
</synced_block>
where $`\eta`$ is a possible phase factor that (by the previous argument about observables) should satisfy $`\eta ^ { 2 } = \pm 1`$ . We could, in principle, assign different phase factors to the $`b`$ and $`d`$ operators, but we choose them to be the same so that the parity transformation is compatible with the Majorana condition $`d _ { s } ( \mathbf { p } ) = b _ { s } ( \mathbf { p } )`$ . Writing the mode expansion of the free field
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#1ebd118f5c0e4d3b85084927362a52b3">
	$$
	\Psi ( x ) = \sum _ { s = \pm } \int \widetilde { d p } \left[ b _ { s } ( \mathbf { p } ) u _ { s } ( \mathbf { p } ) e ^ { i p x } + d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( \mathbf { p } ) v _ { s } ( \mathbf { p } ) e ^ { - i p x } \right] , \tag{40.11}
	$$
</synced_block>
the parity transformation reads
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#aedeb784801a48e18fee428a2fae6c71">
	$$
	\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle { \cal P } ^ { - 1 } \Psi ( x ) { \cal P } } } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ = \sum _ { s = \pm } \int \widetilde { d p } \left[ \left( { \cal P } ^ { - 1 } b _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) { \cal P } \right) u _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { i p x } + \left( { \cal P } ^ { - 1 } d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) { \cal P } \right) v _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { - i p x } \right] } } \\{ ~ = \displaystyle \sum _ { s = \pm } \int \widetilde { d p } \left[ \eta ^ { * } b _ { s } ( - { \bf p } ) u _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { i p x } + \eta d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( - { \bf p } ) v _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { - i p x } \right] } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ = \sum _ { s = \pm } \int \widetilde { d p } \left[ \eta ^ { * } b _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) u _ { s } ( - { \bf p } ) e ^ { i p \tilde { P } x } + \eta d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) v _ { s } ( - { \bf p } ) e ^ { - i p \tilde { P } x } \right] . ~ } } \end{array} \tag{40.12}
	$$
</synced_block>
In the last line, we have changed the integration from $`\mathbf { p }`$ to $`- \mathbf { p }`$ . We now use a result from section 38, namely that
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#af1788440ad74fe5b706b6df3410901f">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r } { u _ { s } ( - \mathbf { p } ) = + \beta u _ { s } ( \mathbf { p } ) \ , } \\{ v _ { s } ( - \mathbf { p } ) = - \beta v _ { s } ( \mathbf { p } ) \ , } \end{array} \tag{40.13}
	$$
</synced_block>
where
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#63ae34704d9d4bda860704d240990e4b">
	$$
	\beta = { \binom { 0 } { I } } \ { \binom { I } { \ 0 } } \ . \tag{40.14}
	$$
</synced_block>
Then, if we choose $`\eta = - i`$ , eq. (40.12) becomes
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#2552a1e950174e4398fef36273075424">
		$$
		\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle { \cal P } ^ { - 1 } \Psi ( x ) { \cal P } } } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ = \sum _ { s = \pm } \int \widetilde { d p } \left[ \left( { \cal P } ^ { - 1 } b _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) { \cal P } \right) u _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { i p x } + \left( { \cal P } ^ { - 1 } d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) { \cal P } \right) v _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { - i p x } \right] } } \\{ ~ = \displaystyle \sum _ { s = \pm } \int \widetilde { d p } \left[ \eta ^ { * } b _ { s } ( - { \bf p } ) u _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { i p x } + \eta d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( - { \bf p } ) v _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { - i p x } \right] } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ = \sum _ { s = \pm } \int \widetilde { d p } \left[ \eta ^ { * } b _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) u _ { s } ( - { \bf p } ) e ^ { i p \tilde { P } x } + \eta d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) v _ { s } ( - { \bf p } ) e ^ { - i p \tilde { P } x } \right] . ~ } } \end{array} \tag{40.12}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#4793005b17e04c36b44adcc39b651e58">
	$$
	\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle P ^ { - 1 } \Psi ( x ) P = \sum _ { s = \pm } \int \widetilde { d p } \left[ i b _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) \beta u _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { i p \mathcal { P } x } + i d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) \beta v _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { - i p \mathcal { P } x } \right] } } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ } } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ = i \beta \Psi ( { \mathcal P } x ) ~ . } } \end{array} \tag{40.15}
	$$
</synced_block>
Thus we see that $`D ( \mathcal { P } ) = i \beta`$ . (We could also have chosen $`\eta = i`$ , resulting in $`D ( \mathcal { P } ) = - i \beta`$ ; either choice is acceptable.)
The factor of $`i`$ has an interesting physical consequence. Consider a state of an electron and positron with zero center-of-mass momentum,
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#e724cbde196843dc9f1d4e6efa9f6ca5">
	$$
	| \phi \rangle = \int \widetilde { d p } \phi ( { \bf p } ) b _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) d _ { s ^ { \prime } } ^ { \dagger } ( - { \bf p } ) | 0 \rangle ; \tag{40.16}
	$$
</synced_block>
here $`\phi ( \mathbf { p } )`$ is the momentum-space wave function. Let us assume that the vacuum is parity invariant: $`P | 0 \rangle = P ^ { - 1 } | 0 \rangle = | 0 \rangle`$ . Let us also assume that the wave function has definite parity: $`\phi ( - { \bf p } ) = ( - ) ^ { \ell } \phi ( { \bf p } )`$ . Then, applying the inverse parity operator on $`| \phi \rangle`$ , we get
$$
\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle P ^ { - 1 } | \phi \rangle = \int \widetilde { d p } \phi ( { \bf p } ) \Big ( P ^ { - 1 } b _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) P \Big ) \Big ( P ^ { - 1 } d _ { s ^ { \prime } } ^ { \dagger } ( - { \bf p } ) P \Big ) P ^ { - 1 } | 0 \rangle . } } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ = ( - i ) ^ { 2 } \int \widetilde { d p } \phi ( { \bf p } ) b _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( - { \bf p } ) d _ { s ^ { \prime } } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) | 0 \rangle } } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ = ( - i ) ^ { 2 } \int \widetilde { d p } \phi ( - { \bf p } ) b _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) d _ { s ^ { \prime } } ^ { \dagger } ( - { \bf p } ) | 0 \rangle } } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ = - ( - ) ^ { \ell } | \phi \rangle ~ . } } \end{array}
$$
Thus, the parity of this state is opposite to that of its wave function; an electron-positron pair has an intrinsic parity of $`- 1`$ . This also applies to a pair of Majorana fermions. This influences the selection rules for fermion pair annihilation in theories that conserve parity. (A pair of electrons also has negative intrinsic parity, but this is less interesting because the electrons are prevented from annihilating by charge conservation.)
Let us see what eq. (40.15) implies for the two Weyl fields that comprise the Dirac field. Recalling that
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#21f822899e354342babfed6418f07442">
		$$
		\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle P ^ { - 1 } \Psi ( x ) P = \sum _ { s = \pm } \int \widetilde { d p } \left[ i b _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) \beta u _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { i p \mathcal { P } x } + i d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) \beta v _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { - i p \mathcal { P } x } \right] } } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ } } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ = i \beta \Psi ( { \mathcal P } x ) ~ . } } \end{array} \tag{40.15}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#1611c5440da24a57bcda10d5983c7c4f">
	$$
	\Psi = \left( { \chi \atop \xi ^ { \dagger \dot { a } } } \right) , \tag{40.18}
	$$
</synced_block>
we see from eqs. (40.14) and (40.15) that
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#790b6789bf274f859d4c4893a756fa8e">
		$$
		\beta = { \binom { 0 } { I } } \ { \binom { I } { \ 0 } } \ . \tag{40.14}
		$$
	</synced_block>
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#6f65fd906adc4084ae19480f362fec0d">
		$$
		\begin{array} { l } { { \displaystyle P ^ { - 1 } \Psi ( x ) P = \sum _ { s = \pm } \int \widetilde { d p } \left[ i b _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) \beta u _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { i p \mathcal { P } x } + i d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) \beta v _ { s } ( { \bf p } ) e ^ { - i p \mathcal { P } x } \right] } } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ } } \\{ { \displaystyle ~ = i \beta \Psi ( { \mathcal P } x ) ~ . } } \end{array} \tag{40.15}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#a7e4a0e88f3a49cbb7bd59fd3a26a70b">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r c l } { { } } & { { } } & { { P ^ { - 1 } \chi _ { a } ( x ) P = i \xi ^ { \dagger \dot { a } } ( \mathcal { P } x ) , } } \\{ { } } & { { } } & { { } } \\{ { } } & { { } } & { { P ^ { - 1 } \xi ^ { \dagger \dot { a } } ( x ) P = i \chi _ { a } ( \mathcal { P } x ) . } } \end{array} \tag{40.19}
	$$
</synced_block>
Thus a parity transformation exchanges a left-handed field for a righthanded one.
If we take the hermitian conjugate of eq. (40.19), then raise the index on one side while lowering it on the other (and remember that this introduces a relative minus sign!), we get
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#4e41499f06fe4f5fad90669b40ca6456">
		$$
		\begin{array} { r c l } { { } } & { { } } & { { P ^ { - 1 } \chi _ { a } ( x ) P = i \xi ^ { \dagger \dot { a } } ( \mathcal { P } x ) , } } \\{ { } } & { { } } & { { } } \\{ { } } & { { } } & { { P ^ { - 1 } \xi ^ { \dagger \dot { a } } ( x ) P = i \chi _ { a } ( \mathcal { P } x ) . } } \end{array} \tag{40.19}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#e9ba7743da4b46faa5863b806b09b00a">
	$$
	\begin{array} { l } { { P ^ { - 1 } \chi ^ { \dagger \dot { a } } ( x ) P = i \xi _ { a } ( \mathcal { P } x ) \ , } } \\{ { { } } } \\{ { P ^ { - 1 } \xi _ { a } ( x ) P = i \chi ^ { \dagger \dot { a } } ( \mathcal { P } x ) \ . } } \end{array} \tag{40.20}
	$$
</synced_block>
Comparing eqs. (40.19) and (40.20), we see that they are compatible with the Majorana condition $`\chi _ { a } ( x ) = \xi _ { a } ( x )`$ .
<callout color="gray_bg">
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#ed292350e3b3441f976c447a755bc523">
		$$
		\begin{array} { r c l } { { } } & { { } } & { { P ^ { - 1 } \chi _ { a } ( x ) P = i \xi ^ { \dagger \dot { a } } ( \mathcal { P } x ) , } } \\{ { } } & { { } } & { { } } \\{ { } } & { { } } & { { P ^ { - 1 } \xi ^ { \dagger \dot { a } } ( x ) P = i \chi _ { a } ( \mathcal { P } x ) . } } \end{array} \tag{40.19}
		$$
	</synced_block>
	<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#85de1ec637174e85b7366c38f0543036">
		$$
		\begin{array} { l } { { P ^ { - 1 } \chi ^ { \dagger \dot { a } } ( x ) P = i \xi _ { a } ( \mathcal { P } x ) \ , } } \\{ { { } } } \\{ { P ^ { - 1 } \xi _ { a } ( x ) P = i \chi ^ { \dagger \dot { a } } ( \mathcal { P } x ) \ . } } \end{array} \tag{40.20}
		$$
	</synced_block>
</callout>
Next we take up time reversal. Define the time-reversal transformation
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#bf2e82c7313744f4bb9cb5a11c585bff">
	$$
	T ^ { \mu } { } _ { \nu } = ( T ^ { - 1 } ) ^ { \mu } { } _ { \nu } = \left( \begin{array} { c c c c } { { - 1 } } & { { } } & { { } } & { { } } \\{ { } } & { { + 1 } } & { { } } & { { } } \\{ { } } & { { } } & { { + 1 } } & { { } } \\{ { } } & { { } } & { { } } & { { + 1 } } \end{array} \right) \tag{40.21}
	$$
</synced_block>
and the corresponding operator
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#1867cafc77f74715979f3e8c56588253">
	$$
	T \equiv U ( \tau ) . \tag{40.22}
	$$
</synced_block>
Now we have
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#5faf9aa3761c4e0898b9ad232b7d5c94">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r } { T ^ { - 1 } \Psi ( x ) T = D ( T ) \Psi ( T x ) . } \end{array} \tag{40.23}
	$$
</synced_block>
The question we wish to answer is, what is the matrix $`D ( \mathcal { T } )`$ ?
As with parity, we can conclude that $`D ( \mathcal { T } ) ^ { 2 } = \pm 1`$ , and we will require the particle creation and annihilation operators to transform in a simple way. Because
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#ad5edc8500874b34986be46e475cf074">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r } { T ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { P } T = - \mathbf { P } \ , } \\{ T ^ { - 1 } \mathbf { J } T = - \mathbf { J } \ , } \end{array} \tag{40.24-40.25}
	$$
</synced_block>
where $`\mathbf { P }`$ is the total three-momentum operator and $`\mathbf { J }`$ is the total angular momentum operator, a time-reversal transformation should reverse the direction of both the three-momentum and the spin. We therefore require
<synced_block url="https://app.notion.com/p/c9cbde61fce8474281189008cfa39813#39ec4177d26e4618ab897df8bbfe007e">
	$$
	\begin{array} { r } { T ^ { - 1 } b _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) T = \zeta _ { s } b _ { - s } ^ { \dagger } ( - { \bf p } ) , } \\{ T ^ { - 1 } d _ { s } ^ { \dagger } ( { \bf p } ) T = \zeta _ { s } d _ { - s } ^ { \dagger } ( - { \bf p } ) . } \end{array} \tag{40.26}
	$$
</synced_block>
This time we allow for possible $`s`$ -dependence of the phase factor. Also, we recall from section 23 that $`T`$ must be an antiunitary operator, so that $`T ^ { - 1 } i T = - i`$ . Then we have
$$

where we have used $`{ \mathcal P } ^ { \mu } { } _ { \nu } T ^ { \nu } { } _ { \rho } = - \delta ^ { \mu } { } _ { \rho }`$ . We see that $`{ \overline { { \Psi } } } \Psi`$ and $`\overline { { \Psi } } i \gamma _ { 5 } \Psi`$ are both even under $`C P T`$ , while $`{ \overline { { \Psi } } } \gamma ^ { \mu } \Psi`$ and $`{ \overline { { \Psi } } } \gamma ^ { \mu } \gamma _ { 5 } \Psi`$ are both odd. These are (it turns out) examples of a more general rule: a fermion bilinear with $`n`$ vector indices (and no uncontracted spinor indices) is even (odd) under $`C P T`$ if $`n`$ is even (odd). This also applies if we allow derivatives acting on the fields, since each component of $`\partial _ { \mu }`$ is odd under the combination $`P T`$ and even under $`C`$ .
For scalar and vector fields, it is always possible to choose the phase factors in the $`C`$ , $`P`$ , and $`T`$ transformations so that, overall, they obey the same rule: a hermitian combination of fields and derivatives is even or odd depending on the total number of uncontracted vector indices. Putting this together with our result for fermion bilinears, we see that any hermitian combination of any set of fields (scalar, vector, Dirac, Majorana) and their derivatives that is a Lorentz scalar (and so carries no indices) is even under $`C P T`$ . Since the lagrangian must be formed out of such combinations, we have $`{ \mathcal { L } } ( x ) \to { \mathcal { L } } ( - x )`$ under $`C P T`$ , and so the action $`\textstyle S = \int d ^ { 4 } x { \mathcal { L } }`$ is invariant. This is the $`C P T`$ theorem.
Reference notes
A detailed treatment of $`C P T`$ for fields of any spin is given in Weinberg I.
## Problems
### 40.1
Find the transformation properties of $`{ \overline { { \Psi } } } S ^ { \mu \nu } \Psi`$ and $`{ \overline { { \Psi } } } i S ^ { \mu \nu } \gamma _ { 5 } \Psi`$ under $`P`$ , $`T`$ , and $`C`$ . Verify that they are both even under $`C P T`$ , as claimed. Do either or both vanish if $`\Psi`$ is a Majorana field?
